prompt: Which gap left by digital signatures does a public key infrastructure close?

choices.text: Signatures are too slow for the web
choices.why: Speed was not the problem named.

choices.text: Knowing whose public key you hold
choices.why: Right. A third party both trust vouches for the binding.

choices.text: Signatures do not encrypt the message
choices.why: A PKI does not add encryption to a signature.

choices.text: A private key has to be sent to the other party first
choices.why: A private key is never sent; the public one is the question.

prompt: A phishing site at a lookalike name shows a valid padlock. What has its certificate established?
hint: Read the right-hand column of the table.

choices.text: That the CA judged the site legitimate
choices.why: A CA checks control of a name, not honesty.

choices.text: Nothing: a CA refuses lookalike names
choices.why: It checks control of the name that was asked for.

choices.text: That the connection reaches the lookalike name
choices.why: Right. The padlock says nothing about the name itself.

choices.text: That no other certificate exists for that same name
choices.why: A certificate does not say that.

prompt: Which of these does a certificate state? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The key's holder controlled the name when it was issued
choices.why: Right. At issue, not today.

choices.text: The key is still in the right hands today
choices.why: It cannot know; that is what revocation is for.

choices.text: The CA checked that control as its policy says
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The binding holds between two dates
choices.why: Right: notBefore and notAfter.

choices.text: The site behind the name is safe to use
choices.why: Safety is not what a CA checks.

prompt: Match each of the company's certificates to what it may sign.
right_distractors: other roots, and nothing below them

prompt: The root's subject and issuer are the same. What makes laptop trust it?

choices.text: The issuing CA vouches for it
choices.why: The arrow points the other way.

choices.text: Its signature checks against its own key
choices.why: Anybody's self-made root would pass that.

choices.text: CA:TRUE in its Basic Constraints
choices.why: That says what it may sign, not who believes it.

choices.text: It is in the trust store
choices.why: Right. Nothing vouches for a root.

prompt: Why does the root sign the issuing CA once and then go offline instead of signing servers every day?

choices.text: Losing its key means reconfiguring every machine that trusts it
choices.why: Right. An issuing CA's loss is repaired by the root.

choices.text: pathlen:0 stops it signing servers
choices.why: pathlen:0 is on the issuing CA.

choices.text: A root's signatures are slower
choices.why: The cost is risk, not speed.

choices.text: Its ten years would outlive the servers
choices.why: A certificate's own dates are set per certificate.

prompt: openssl verify was given the root as trusted and www.example.com.crt, with no intermediate. Which error number did it print?
hint: unable to get local issuer certificate.

prompt: In the chain www.example.com sent to laptop, which certificate was missing, and why?

choices.text: The issuing CA, since laptop already has it
choices.why: Depth 1 was the issuing CA.

choices.text: The root, from laptop's own store
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The server's own, cached from last time
choices.why: Depth 0 was the server's certificate.

choices.text: None was missing: all three were sent
choices.why: Only two lines came back.

prompt: Why is the intermediate passed to openssl verify with -untrusted rather than added to -CAfile?
hint: Which certificates are believed on their own?

choices.text: -CAfile accepts one file
choices.why: The chain.pem in the revocation section held two.

choices.text: An intermediate has no signature to check
choices.why: The root signed it, and that is checked.

choices.text: It is verified on the way up
choices.why: Right. Roots are trusted; intermediates are verified.

choices.text: -untrusted makes openssl skip its dates
choices.why: Its dates are checked like any other link's.

prompt: openssl printed 'Certificate request self-signature verify OK' for app.csr. What does that establish?

choices.text: The CA has approved the request
choices.why: Nothing has reached the CA yet.

choices.text: Its maker holds the private key matching the public key inside
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The requester controls app.corp.example.com
choices.why: Checking the name is the CA's job, afterwards.

choices.text: The issuing CA's key signed it
choices.why: The CA signs the certificate, not the request.

prompt: Order the issuance of app's certificate, from first to last.
items: app makes its key and a signing request
the CA checks the requester against its process
the CA signs with its own extensions and dates
a V line for the new serial joins the register
trap: Deciding whether to sign comes before signing; the register records what was signed.

prompt: Which serial number did the CA give app.corp.example.com's certificate?
Public CAs check control of the name, then issue automatically through the ___ protocol.
After serial 1003 was revoked, which error number did openssl verify -crl_check print for app.crt?
The CRL's Next Update is seven days after its Last Update. What does that date mean?

choices.text: Revoked serials drop off the list on that day
choices.why: A revocation stays listed; the list is renewed.

choices.text: Certificate 1003 becomes valid again after that date
choices.why: Revocation is not a suspension here.

choices.text: Clients keep it until then, when a new one is due
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The CA's key expires on that date
choices.why: The issuing CA runs until 2031.

prompt: Match each revocation mechanism to its weakness.

pairs.right: lists grow large and clients skip them
the CA learns what everyone visits
helps only if the client insists on it

right_distractors: the root has to come back online

prompt: Why can a company's CA make revocation work where the public web struggles?

choices.text: Internal CRLs are small enough to fetch each time
choices.why: Size is not what makes clients check.

choices.text: Internal certificates last longer
choices.why: A longer life makes revocation matter more.

choices.text: OCSP does not work on internal names
choices.why: It does; that is not the reason.

choices.text: It controls both ends, so clients must check
choices.why: Right. Every client checks the CRL and refuses when it cannot.

prompt: What does a name constraint of corp.example.com change about installing the company CA on staff laptops?
hint: Which names can it vouch for?

choices.text: Public sites are safe from it
choices.why: Right. The CA vouches only for the company's names.

choices.text: The laptops stop needing a trust store
choices.why: The root still has to be installed.

choices.text: Revocation becomes unnecessary
choices.why: A stolen key inside the domain still needs taking back.

choices.text: Staff can reach corp.example.com from home
choices.why: Constraints limit signing, not reachability.

prompt: According to the section, which PKI failure is far more common than any attack?

choices.text: A root key copied off a disk
choices.why: Keys in hardware answer that, and it is rarer.

choices.text: A forgotten certificate expiring
choices.why: Right. An inventory answers it.

choices.text: A CA signing a request it should have refused
choices.why: A written policy answers that, and it is rarer.

choices.text: An internal CA used to impersonate a public site
choices.why: Name constraints answer that.

prompt: What does monitoring Certificate Transparency logs give the company?

choices.text: It stops any CA issuing for its names
choices.why: Logs record issuance; they do not prevent it.

choices.text: It revokes unrequested certificates at once
choices.why: Revoking is the issuing CA's act.

choices.text: Word within hours of a certificate for its names it did not ask for
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A copy of every private key for its domains
choices.why: Logs hold certificates, never keys.

prompt: After a web server is reinstalled, browsers that visited before still connect, but new clients fail with 'unable to get local issuer certificate'. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Error 20, seen from the server's side.

choices.text: The root was removed from the new clients' trust stores
choices.why: Then the old visitors would fail too.

choices.text: The server's certificate has expired
choices.why: That would fail every client, with a different error.

choices.text: It no longer sends the intermediate
choices.why: Right. Clients that have seen it before fill the gap.

choices.text: Its certificate was revoked
choices.why: Revocation is error 23, for old and new clients alike.

prompt: The issuing CA's key is stolen. What has to change on the staff laptops' trust stores?
hint: What do the laptops actually trust?

choices.text: The root is replaced on each one
choices.why: That is the price of losing the root, not the issuing CA.

choices.text: Nothing: the root replaces the issuing CA
choices.why: Right. The servers get new certificates; the stores stay as they are.

choices.text: The issuing CA is added to each, as trusted
choices.why: Intermediates are verified, not trusted.

choices.text: The stolen key's fingerprint is blocked in each
choices.why: Trust stores hold roots, not a blocklist; a CRL carries the revocation.

prompt: An old monitoring agent never fetches CRLs and cannot be changed. Which practice limits how long a stolen service key stays useful against it?
hint: Which defence does not depend on the client checking?

choices.text: Publishing the CRL more frequently
choices.why: It never reads one, however fresh.

choices.text: Keeping the root offline
choices.why: That protects the root, not a service key.

choices.text: Name constraints on the issuing CA
choices.why: The stolen certificate is inside the allowed names.

choices.text: Short certificate lifetimes
choices.why: Right. The certificate expires on schedule, checked or not.
